summary: Describes the features of the computerised facsimile system developed at University College London, covering its functions, related experiments, design principles and implementation. Detailed descriptions are given in appendices.

eli5.summary: A university team built a system for sending fax pages with computers. This memo describes what it does and how they made it.

subtitle: A computerized facsimile system for sending and manipulating document images over networks.

tldr.problem: Facsimile machines could only exchange images via telephone lines with identical equipment, could not store or edit pages, and were incompatible across different manufacturers.
tldr.mechanism: University College London developed a system combining an LSI-11 microcomputer, fax machine, disk storage, and a Grinnell color display to receive fax pages, store them on disk, manipulate images, and transmit them over computer networks like ARPANET/SATNET.
tldr.outcome: The system demonstrated that facsimile machines could integrate with computer networks, support image format conversion, enable bitmap editing, and combine images with text, laying groundwork for future multimedia document systems.

today: RFC 809 describes a pioneering implementation. Modern facsimile systems adopted digital storage, format conversion, and network transmission as standard features. However, the system's vision of integrating fax with other document types matured into MIME (Multipurpose Internet Mail Extensions) and modern office document formats. The three-layer architecture and Clean and Simple interface concept influenced later modular and pipeline-based systems. Today, facsimile itself has largely been superseded by email-based document transmission and digital signatures, though the principles of image compression, format conversion, and network transmission remain fundamental to document handling systems.

sections.title: Facsimile Meets Computing
sections.content:
Facsimile (fax) machines had been used since 1843 to transmit document images over distance, but they were designed exclusively for telephone networks. A standard fax machine at the time could not store pages, could not modify images, and could not communicate with different manufacturers' equipment—two machines from different companies simply would not understand each other.

The Department of Computer Science at University College London undertook to apply computer technology to facsimile. Rather than a phone-based point-to-point link, a computer could store fax data, convert between formats, improve image quality, enable editing, and transmit over networks like ARPANET/SATNET. The system used an LSI-11 microcomputer running the MOS operating system, a DACOM 6450 facsimile machine, AED62 floppy disks for storage, and a Grinnell color display for viewing and editing images.
sections.eli5: Fax machines could only talk to each other over phone lines and had to be the same brand. Researchers wanted to use computers to send fax pictures over computer networks and improve them along the way.

sections.title: Network Transmission and Image Buffering
sections.content:
The first challenge was that facsimile machines transmit data at a constant, high rate—the DACOM 6450 sent data faster than the ARPANET/SATNET network could reliably accept. When the network delayed data, the facsimile machine interpreted this as a communication failure and abandoned the transfer mid-page.

The solution was local buffering. Instead of streaming data directly to the network, the system worked in three stages: first, capture the fax data at high speed into local disk storage; second, transmit the stored data over the network at whatever speed the network could sustain; third, output the received data to the destination fax machine. This decoupled the facsimile machine from network delays. The system successfully exchanged pictures between UCL in London, ISI in Los Angeles, and COMSAT in Washington D.C. using NIFTP (Network Independent File Transfer Protocol) over ARPANET/SATNET.

The disadvantage was that senders no longer knew when pages would arrive at the destination. But when many operators sent to the same destination, the system could queue pages, allowing all of them to input quickly without waiting for the remote machine to become free—an improvement over the existing phone system.
sections.eli5: The network couldn't keep up with the fax machine's speed, so the system saved pages to disk first, then sent them over the network at whatever pace was possible. This let the fax machine finish quickly even if the network was slow.

sections.title: Format Conversion and Image Enhancement
sections.content:
A major innovation was format conversion. Because the system had image data in digital form on disk, it could decompress DACOM-format data, convert it to an internal vector format (a line-by-line representation), recompress it for a different fax machine, and transmit it. This enabled machines from different manufacturers to exchange images despite proprietary compression methods.

The team also developed the CCITT T.4 compression algorithms, the new international standard for fax, proving that data conversion could be done on a small computer. Though no test partners had CCITT-capable machines at the time, this capability showed the path forward.

For image enhancement, the system could clean up noisy scans of printed documents. The enhancement algorithm examined each pixel and, based on surrounding pixels, could smooth rough edges caused by scanner noise. This produced cleaner images, higher compression ratios, and better readability—though the system learned that improving readability was harder than improving compression efficiency.

Display on the Grinnell screen required handling resolution mismatches: the DACOM machine produced 1726 dots across a page, but the screen only had 512 pixels. The system developed a thinning algorithm that reduced the number of dots without destroying important image features like lines in architectural drawings. By duplicating pixels or using iterative enlargement, images could be resized for display or printed at different scales.
sections.eli5: The system converted pictures from one fax format to another so different brand machines could exchange images. It could also clean up blurry scan copies and resize pictures to fit on screens or paper without losing the important details.

sections.title: Image Editing and Multimedia Integration
sections.content:
The system supported interactive image editing on the color display. Users could select rectangular areas of one image and move them onto another using a color-highlighted cursor controlled by keyboard commands. The editor maintained a scaled copy for interactive display while performing actual edits on full-resolution data. This enabled cutting, merging, and compositing multiple images—operations impossible with a traditional fax machine.

Beyond fax images, the system integrated text and graphics. Text strings could be converted to bitmap format (as a software font) and mixed with pictures to create composite documents. This early exploration of combining multiple data types in a single document prefigured MIME-based multimedia email.

Moreover, the system supported multiple output devices: pages could print on the DACOM fax machine, display on the Grinnell color screen, or be stored as image files on disk. This flexibility suggested that facsimile machines could become networked output devices for any digital document—like printers today.
sections.eli5: Users could edit pictures by choosing parts of one image and pasting them onto another using the color screen. Text could be converted to look like it was in the picture. Images could be printed, displayed, or saved to disk.

sections.title: System Design: Hierarchical Multi-Task Architecture
sections.content:
The system was organized in three layers. At the bottom were device drivers handling physical I/O for the fax machine, disk, display, and network. In the middle were task processes—independent MOS processes implementing file system access, image decompression/recompression, image manipulation (chop, scale, merge, clean), format conversion, and network transmission. At the top was a task controller that assembled task processes into execution chains based on command strings.

The key insight was the Clean and Simple interface: a standardized way for tasks to pass data. Rather than tasks writing temporary files or managing their own buffers, the interface routines handled signal handling, buffer management, and synchronization. Data moved through the chain as line vectors (compressed rows of image data), making the system modular and flexible.

Command strings specified a task pipeline using pipe notation (like Unix shells): fax"r|fs"c,doc meant read from the facsimile machine and create a file named "doc" in the file system. The task controller would parse the command, link the tasks, and execute them. This made complex jobs easy to express without writing code.
sections.eli5: The system worked like an assembly line: each task did one simple job, and data flowed between tasks through standard interfaces. A command string like a recipe told the system which tasks to run in what order.

sections.title: Challenges and Future Directions
sections.content:
The experimental system faced practical limitations. Network throughput over ARPANET/SATNET was only about 500 bits per second, taking at least 5 minutes to transmit one page—a stark reminder that the network was not designed for image data. The LSI-11's small primary memory meant not all system modules could be loaded simultaneously; the team had to load separate systems for editing and for network transmission.

Image processing was slow—scaling a picture to fit the screen took several minutes. The floppy disk storage (630K bytes per drive) could hold only a limited number of image files. These constraints motivated the vision of a distributed system where a passive facsimile server (the LSI-11 with fax and display) could be controlled remotely by a UNIX host with large disks and faster processing.

The system demonstrated the core idea: facsimile could evolve from a point-to-point telephone service into a networked multimedia system integrated with computers. Future work would require addressing storage capacity, processing speed, and standardized data formats—all problems that modern systems solved through advances in hardware and protocols like MIME.
sections.eli5: The system was slow and limited by small disk space and memory. The researchers imagined a future where a fax machine would be controlled by a bigger, faster computer that could handle all the image processing and file storage.
